title: Green ash chair spindle
subtitle: Green-woodwork: drawknife and sloyd knife shaping of a spindle back chair rung
excerpt: A single back spindle for a Windsor-style chair, shaped from a riven green ash billet with a drawknife and sloyd knife. The spindle is round-tapered at both ends to fit bored socket holes in the seat and the bow. Making spindles is the core skill of pole-lathe turning and can be practised by hand before investing in a lathe.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for Windsor spindle shaping; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the drawknife taper method on green timber.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled wood, still moist. The drawknife cuts green ash cleanly; the spindle is then dried before the tenon ends are fitted to prevent the joint loosening.
Split along the grain with a froe and mallet. Riven sections follow the grain perfectly; a sawn spindle has cross-grain at some point and will snap under side load.
A leg-operated bench vice used for drawknife work; the foot pedal clamps the work and frees both hands for the tool.
A two-handled blade pulled toward the body for rapid wood removal; the main tool for spindle shaping.

content.text: A chair spindle is a slender tapered rod, round in cross-section, that fits a bored hole at each end. The Windsor chair pattern uses seven to nine spindles in the back; the technique for making one is the same whether you are making one or nine. A well-made green ash spindle,
rather than sawn, follows the grain its full length and does not snap under back-load. Sawn spindles are fine for show chairs; riven spindles are for chairs that get daily use.
. Source a straight-grained ash log; ash splits cleanly and the drawknife removes material fast while the wood is green.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.

One riven green ash billet, 50 cm long, 3 cm square section. The grain must run along the full length with no runout. Ash is preferred for spindles because it has outstanding resistance to splitting along the grain under side load. Sycamore or birch work but are stiffer and less resilient.
Froe and beetle mallet for riving the billet.
Shaving horse for holding the work.
A shaving horse outdoors or in a workshop. The drawknife needs about 50 cm of clear swing in front of the work.

Split the ash log with the froe to produce a 3 cm square billet. Quarter the log first, then rive the quarters to the right section size. Check the grain runs along the length, this is the whole point of riving.

to take the four corners off the square section, producing an octagon. Work along the grain, reading the surface after each pass: smooth means with the grain, rough means against it. Reverse direction when the surface lifts.

Continue with the drawknife to remove the eight corners of the octagon, bringing the section to sixteen-sided, then to round. Aim for 18 mm diameter at the centre. Work the ends down to 15 mm for the last 5 cm of each end, this is the tenon diameter for the socket holes.
Step 4: Refine with the sloyd knife

to smooth any flat facets left by the drawknife, and to refine the tenon diameter to a consistent 15 mm. Test the tenon against a 15 mm socket, it should go in with hand pressure and light friction. If it goes in easily, pare a whisker of the billet diameter to bring the tenon closer to 14 mm; the joint tightens as the spindle dries in the socket.

Hang the finished spindle in a warm, dry place for two weeks before fitting it. As it dries, the tenon diameter shrinks slightly. The socket in the chair seat is bored while the spindle is dry, the tenon then fits the socket with the tightest possible joint.
Stool stretcher: 40 cm long, 22 mm body diameter. Same method.
Rake handle: 120 cm, 25 mm diameter throughout. Rive from a longer log section.

attrs.symptom: The drawknife digs in and tears chunks rather than shaving
attrs.cause: Going against the grain, the drawknife is pulling toward the end where the grain runs downhill from the surface
attrs.fix: Reverse direction and pull from the other end of the billet. In green ash the grain-direction changes are visible as subtle colour bands on the surface. Sight along the surface after each pass to check.
